title: A Touch on the Hollow of the Thigh — Fear, Wrestling, a Limp
blocks: Peace to you, brothers and sisters. What we come to today is the most decisive night in the whole book of Genesis — and the hinge on which Jacob's entire life turns.

He has left Laban behind him, and he is on the road home. And what is waiting for him up ahead is the brother who swore twenty years ago that he would kill him, coming out to meet him with four hundred men.
So the question this lesson puts to us is this: when God means to deal with a man, how long does he wait before he moves?
And this chapter gives a very clear answer. He waits until that man has nothing left in his hands to manage with.

Let me put the answer right at the front: the way to win is to admit that you have lost. The moment he was called Israel is the very moment he said, "My name is Jacob" — and that limping leg was the greatest blessing of his life.
1. He Saw God's Army, and Was Frightened Anyway
Verse 1: "Jacob went on his way, and the angels of God met him."
Brothers and sisters, "went on his way" is הָלַךְ לְדַרְכּוֹ — he walked his own road. It is the most ordinary sentence imaginable. And the miracle happens on the ordinary road.
And "met him" is וַיִּפְגְּעוּ־בוֹ, literally "they ran into him" — the same verb that Genesis 28:11 uses when Jacob "came upon" that place which became Bethel.
Verse 2: "When he saw them, Jacob said, 'This is God's army.' He called the name of that place Mahanaim."
"Mahanaim", מַחֲנָיִם, is a dual form. It means "two camps" — God's camp and Jacob's camp, the two of them standing side by side.
Brothers and sisters, he saw God's army first.
Then in verse 6 the messengers come back and say, "We came to your brother Esau. He is coming to meet you, and four hundred men are with him."
Verse 7: "Then Jacob was greatly afraid and was distressed."
Brothers and sisters, please lay verse 2 and verse 7 side by side. He has only just seen the camp of God; the next moment he hears "four hundred men" and he is terrified.
And God does not rebuke him.

That is an enormous release for us: a person who has seen God act will still be afraid the next time round. That is not a shortage of faith; that is being human. And God's response is not a scolding — it is to come in person that night and wrestle a round with him.
Your fear will not frighten God away.
He has just seen the camp of God, and one moment later the words "four hundred men" terrify him. Isn't that rather poor faith?

In verse 2 he names the place Mahanaim — a dual form, "two camps". By verse 7 the text says, "Then Jacob was greatly afraid and was distressed." There is very little space in between. And the most striking thing in the passage is this: God says not one word of rebuke. That gives us an enormous release — a person who has seen God act will still be afraid the next time, and that is not a shortage of faith, that is how a human being is put together. Spiritual maturity is not that you stop being afraid; it is that when you are afraid you know where to go. So please do not condemn yourself for being frightened again. There is only one thing worth watching: when the fear comes, do you go and pray first, or do you go and start calculating first?
"The angels of God met him" — what is that doing on his road?

The verb behind "met" (פָּגַע) literally means "to run into", and it is the same verb used in chapter 28, where Jacob "came upon" the place that became Bethel. Which is to say: this was not something he went looking for. It came towards him. And the placing of it is more interesting still. It happens on the stretch of road after he has left Laban and before he has seen Esau — the most uncertain stretch of the whole journey. God very often puts the confirmation in the middle of the road, not at the destination. That is intensely practical for us: if you are walking through a season with nothing behind you and nothing yet in front of you, it is worth looking around on purpose — God may already have set a sign for you on this very stretch of road.
2. A Light from the Original: the First "I Am Not Worthy" in Twenty Years
Verses 9 to 12 are the first complete prayer of Jacob's life, and one of the finest prayers in the whole of Genesis.
"God of my father Abraham, and God of my father Isaac, Yahweh, who said to me, 'Return to your country, and to your relatives, and I will do you good.'"
He takes hold of what God has said first. That is the steadiest place a prayer can begin.

Then verse 10: "I am not worthy of the least of all the loving kindnesses, and of all the truth, which you have shown to your servant; for with just my staff I crossed over this Jordan; and now I have become two companies."
Brothers and sisters, please stop on that sentence.
"I am not worthy of the least" — the Hebrew is קָטֹנְתִּי (*qatonti*), and it means literally "I have become small", "I am too small."

For twenty years this man has said a great many things. He bargained with his brother, he lied to his father, he settled accounts with Laban, he lost his temper with Rachel. And this is the first time he has ever said: I am not worthy.
And the sentence he says next is one of the most moving descriptions any man gives of himself in this book: "for with just my staff I crossed over this Jordan; and now I have become two companies."
He hands the whole twenty years back to God — not to his own peeled branches.
In verse 11 he asks: "Please deliver me from the hand of my brother, from the hand of Esau." And in verse 12 he takes hold of the promise once more: "You said, 'I will surely do you good.'"
Brothers and sisters, that is a complete prayer: take hold of what God has said, own that you are not worthy, put the request into concrete words, and then come back to the promise of God.
"He stayed there that night, and took from that which he had with him a present for Esau, his brother."
He has finished praying, and then he starts arranging. Two hundred female goats, twenty male goats, two hundred ewes … herd after herd, driven out ahead of him with a space between each one.
In verse 20 he says, "I will appease him with the present that goes before me, and afterward I will see his face. Perhaps he will accept me."
"I will appease him with the present" — brothers and sisters, his prayer is real, and his arrangements are real too. The question is which of the two he has laid his hope on.
Making arrangements after you have prayed is not a sin. The question to ask is this: if the arrangements fail, will you still be standing?
He finishes praying and then busies himself with presents and companies. Doesn't that count as unbelief?

Making arrangements after praying is not in itself a sin. Joseph stored grain, Nehemiah carried letters, Paul bought passage on a ship — every one of those is an arrangement. What this chapter asks us is a different question: which side is your hope resting on? In verse 20 he says, "I will appease him with the present that goes before me" — and that sentence gives away where his real confidence lies. So the way to check yourself is very simple: if the arrangement fails, will you still be standing? If the answer is "then it is all over", that arrangement has already become the thing you lean on. Here is something practical you can do: each time you finish making a plan, write one line under it — "If this does not work, which word of God do I still have?"
"I am not worthy of the least" — is there something special about that phrase in the original?

The Hebrew is קָטֹנְתִּי (*qatonti*), literally "I have become small", "I am too small." It is the first thing of its kind Jacob has said in twenty years — he had bargained with his brother, lied to his father and settled accounts with Laban, and there was never any shortage of words, but not one of them was "I am not worthy." And then he goes straight on: "for with just my staff I crossed over this Jordan; and now I have become two companies." He hands the whole twenty years back to God. That gives us an excellent pattern for prayer: first take hold of what God has said, then own the truth about yourself, then put the request into concrete words, and finally come back to the promise. Those four steps can be the skeleton of your prayer today.

Verses 22 and 23: "He rose up that night, and took his two wives, and his two servants, and his eleven sons, and crossed over the ford of the Jabbok. … He took them, and sent them over the stream, and sent over that which he had."
Brothers and sisters, count up what he sent away that night. The flocks, sent off. The present, sent off. His wives and his children, sent over the river.
There is nothing left in his hands to manage with.
And the text says he "wrestled with a man there until the breaking of the day."
God waited until this moment to make his move.

This is the most important observation in the chapter: when God means to deal with a man, he waits until that man has no cards left to play. Because as long as there is still one card in the hand, a person goes on calculating, goes on arranging, goes on looking for a way round.
And verse 25: "When he saw that he didn't prevail against him, the man touched the hollow of his thigh, and the hollow of Jacob's thigh was strained as he wrestled."

Brothers and sisters, "he didn't prevail against him" is written from Jacob's point of view. Because the very next clause tells us that he merely "touched" the hollow of the thigh — and that leg was finished.
One touch and the man is left limping. So why wrestle the whole night through?
Because what God wants is not to beat him. It is to have him say it for himself: I cannot win.
And the place he chose to touch was the hollow of the thigh — the strongest place in the human body. God did not break his hands. He took away the strength of his legs.
From that night on he could only lean on a staff. And Hebrews 11:21 says, "By faith Jacob, when he was dying, … worshiped, leaning on the top of his staff."
That staff is the last posture of his life.
If one touch was enough to leave him limping, why wrestle him all night long?

Verse 25 says, "When he saw that he didn't prevail against him, the man touched the hollow of his thigh" — one touch, and a leg was finished, which shows that he had never once been exerting himself. And that phrase "he didn't prevail against him" is written from Jacob's point of view. So the purpose of a whole night of wrestling was not to beat him; it was to bring him to admit for himself that he could not win. This is God's consistent way with people: he is not out to crush anybody, he is waiting for the person to say it out loud. And that is intensely practical for us — if you have been locked in a long stand-off with God over some matter, it is worth asking yourself one question: am I waiting for him to give way, or have I simply not yet said the words "I cannot win"?
Verse 26: "The man said, 'Let me go, for the day breaks.' Jacob said, 'I won't let you go unless you bless me.'"

Brothers and sisters, this man has been grabbing all his life. He came out of the womb with his hand round his brother's heel; he grabbed at the birthright; he grabbed at the blessing; he grabbed at the flocks.
And this time, he grabbed the right thing.
Before, he used schemes to snatch a blessing. Tonight he throws his arms around the One who blesses and will not let go.
Before, what he wanted was the blessing. This time, what he wants is the Person himself.
Then in verse 27 that One asks a question: "What is your name?"
Brothers and sisters, he knows the answer. He asks so that the man will say it himself.
And go back with me to chapter 27. On that day a blind father asked, "Who are you, my son?"
And he said, "I am Esau your firstborn."
Twenty years later the same question is put to him again, in the dark.
And this time he says his own name: "Jacob."
The heel-grabber, the deceiver, the one who takes another man's place — that is exactly what the name means.
At last he has told the truth.
And verse 28: "He said, 'Your name will no longer be called Jacob, but Israel; for you have fought with God and with men, and have prevailed.'"
Brothers and sisters, this is the strangest victory in the whole Bible.
The man who won came away limping. And the way he won was by giving his own real name.
And "Israel", יִשְׂרָאֵל, can be read as "one who strives with God", and it can also be read as "God will fight." From that night on, his own name has the name of God inside it.
Verse 30: "Jacob called the name of the place Peniel; for he said, 'I have seen God face to face, and my life is preserved.'"
Verse 31: "The sun rose on him as he passed over Peniel, and he limped because of his thigh."
The sun came up, and he walked out of there limping.
"What is your name?" — he knew perfectly well. Why ask at all?

Because he wanted the man to say it himself. And that question had been put to him once before, twenty years earlier: on that day a blind father asked, "Who are you, my son?", and he answered, "I am Esau your firstborn." Twenty years later the same question comes again, in the dark, and this time he says his own name — "Jacob": the heel-grabber, the deceiver, the one who takes another man's place. And the blessing is given only after that piece of truth has been spoken. It is the most practical lesson in the chapter: God is not waiting for you to turn into somebody else before he will bless you; he is waiting for you to dare to own who you are. The first step of confession has never been correction. It is giving your name.
5. Distortions You Must Be Able to Spot

The first is preaching the wrestling as though a human being could force God's hand. That line, "when he saw that he didn't prevail against him", is written from Jacob's point of view, and all the man did was touch him once. If you preach it as "the human being beat God", the congregation will start treating prayer as pressure — keep it up long enough, loud enough, stubbornly enough, and God will give in. That is not prayer. That is manipulation.

The second is preaching "I won't let you go unless you bless me" as proof that prayer only works when it is long enough and loud enough. What he took hold of was the Person himself, not a technique. Preach it as a method and prayer turns into the art of negotiation.

The third is preaching the limp as a mark of failure. It was the greatest blessing of his life, and it is the reason he was leaning on a staff to worship at the end of it. Preach it as a loss and your congregation will start dodging God's dealings — and the brothers and sisters who carry a long-standing weakness will walk out under condemnation.

The fourth is preaching the glory of the new name and never mentioning that the very next day he was still dividing his household into groups. In Genesis 33:1–3 he still puts the ones he loves most at the very back. Change is a process; nobody becomes perfect overnight. Preach it as an instantaneous transformation and the congregation will despair of themselves. And notice this too: after that night the text still goes on calling him "Jacob" a great deal of the time — the new name and the old name alternate with each other for a very long while.

The fifth is preaching Genesis 32:32 — "the children of Israel don't eat the sinew of the hip, which is on the hollow of the thigh" — as though it were a law. It is a popular custom that grew out of the story; the Law nowhere legislates it. And what it means is this: a whole nation keeping one habit at the dinner table so as to remember how their forefather came to limp.
6. Two Real Questions from a Chinese Setting

The first question: Chinese culture presses two things on us very hard — you must never admit defeat, and even when you are beaten you must not look beaten. And yet this chapter says the way to win is to admit that you have lost. How do those two talk to each other? Brothers and sisters, this one has to be sorted out very finely. First, the Bible has nothing against tenacity. Jacob wrestled the whole night and never let go — and that is part of the very reason he is called Israel. So the surrender this chapter speaks of is not giving up; it is telling the truth about yourself in front of the right person. Second, everything turns on whom you surrender to. He did not surrender to Esau, and he did not surrender to Laban. He surrendered to God. And it is the man who owns before God that he cannot win who turns out to be able to stand in front of people — the next morning he walked at the head of his whole household to meet his brother (Genesis 33:3), the first time in twenty years that he had not hidden behind somebody else. And third, the most Chinese word in the whole discussion: face. The hardest part of admitting defeat is not admitting the fact; it is admitting it where people can see. And this night happened in a darkness where nobody could see. God is very considerate. He scheduled the hardest lesson for a time when there was no audience.

The second question: I have a long-standing weakness — in my body, in my temperament, in a relationship — and I have prayed about it for years and it has not lifted. Does that mean God is not listening? Brothers and sisters, this chapter gives an answer that is hard and deeply releasing at the same time: some weaknesses are left in place by God's own hand. He touched the hollow of Jacob's thigh, and that leg never got better for the rest of his life. And Hebrews tells us that at the end he worshipped leaning on the top of his staff — and that staff is what that night left him. In 2 Corinthians 12, Paul begged the Lord three times that the thorn might depart from him, and the Lord said to him, "My grace is sufficient for you, for my power is made perfect in weakness." Now I want to say three things very carefully. First, this does not mean that no illness should be prayed over for healing — Scripture tells us to ask. Second, it does not mean that your weakness must have been given to you by God — do not go writing footnotes on other people's suffering. Third: but if you have prayed for a long time and it still has not been taken away, this chapter opens a new possibility for you. It may not be that God has not heard. It may be that he is leaving a staff in your life, so that for as long as you live you will never stand on the strength of your own legs.
I have a weakness I have prayed about for many years and it has never got better. Does that mean my faith is still not enough?

This chapter gives an answer that is hard and deeply releasing at the same time: some weaknesses are left in place by God's own hand. That leg never got better as long as Jacob lived, and the way Hebrews 11 remembers him is that he "worshiped, leaning on the top of his staff" — and that staff is precisely what that night left him. Paul asked three times as well, and the answer he was given was "My grace is sufficient for you." So please do not let anybody tell you that a long-standing weakness is evidence of insufficient faith. And let us be just as clear about the other side: this does not mean you should skip the doctor or refuse treatment. See the doctor you ought to see, take the medicine you ought to take. And the thorn that is still there after you have done everything you ought to do — that is a thorn you may carry with you into worship.
7. Living 321 Out — Wanting Him Himself, Not Only the Good Things in His Hand
Brothers and sisters, let us tie this lesson back into the Three Foundations, the Two Core Values and the Goal of 321.

Jesus is my role model — Hebrews tells us that when Jacob was dying he "worshiped, leaning on the top of his staff." And the Lord Jesus, too, accomplished the greatest victory of all in the place of the greatest weakness; the cross looked like utter defeat. Brothers and sisters, this is my role model: his power is made perfect in weakness.

The Bible is my standard — Jacob's prayer begins from something God had said: "who said to me, 'Return to your country, and to your relatives.'" And he ends by coming back to the very same thing: "You said, 'I will surely do you good.'" That is what a standard is for. On the night you are most frightened, it puts one sentence into your hand that you can hold on to.

The Holy Spirit is my guide — notice the timing of that night. God did not come while Jacob still had flocks, still had schemes, still had arrangements in play. He waited until "Jacob was left alone." Brothers and sisters, if you have lately been stripped down until there is nothing left but yourself, that is not necessarily abandonment. It may be that Someone is drawing near.

Let Jesus be King — "I won't let you go unless you bless me." At last he has grabbed hold of the right thing: before, he wanted the blessing; this time he wants the One who blesses. Letting Jesus be King means wanting him himself, and not only the good things in his hand. Brothers and sisters, here is a very honest test: if God never gave you another good thing as long as you lived, would you still want him?

Let Jesus receive all the glory — that line in verse 10, "I am not worthy of the least of all the loving kindnesses", is the weightiest sentence this man ever spoke. And in Genesis 33:5, when he introduces his children to Esau, he says, "The children whom God has graciously given your servant." He has learned to hand everything back to God.

Establish God's system — the name "Israel" went on to become the name of a whole people. Brothers and sisters, one man's surrender in the dark became the beginning of a nation. Establishing God's system does not start with a successful meeting. It starts with one person admitting defeat on a night when nobody at all was watching.

And here I want to say something honest about 321 itself. We talk a great deal about selflessness, and this chapter gives it its most exact definition: selflessness is not reducing yourself to nothing; it is admitting that I cannot win, and then letting him live inside me. Look at Jacob — he wrestled the whole night, he was thoroughly stubborn, he wanted the blessing. He did not turn into a man with no will of his own. He simply worked out at last whom that strength was meant to be holding on to. So selflessness is not the same as powerlessness. Selflessness is strength that has changed direction.
8. Four Kinds of Heart, One Limping Leg
Brothers and sisters, the same limping leg falls into four different hearts, and each of them sees something different.

The proud heart says, "Jacob finally got what was coming to him." That heart closes the chapter feeling satisfied. Brothers and sisters, notice what kind of night this was — it was not punishment, it was blessing. God did not come to settle the score for what happened twenty years earlier; he came to give the man a new name. And the better question is this: if God asked me tonight, "What is your name?", would I dare tell him the truth?

The fearful heart says, "I don't dare ask God to come and deal with me." That heart is afraid he really will. And to a heart like that I want to say: look at how the night ended — he came away blessed, he came away with a new name, and "my life is preserved." The way God deals with a person is a touch, not a smashing. And the next morning the sun came up.

The ashamed heart says, "I could never say that name of mine out loud." You may be carrying an identity you cannot bring yourself to own — the one who deceived somebody, the one who was a coward, the one who is always calculating. Brothers and sisters, notice this: the blessing was given only after he had said, "My name is Jacob." God is not waiting for you to turn into somebody else before he will bless you. He is waiting for you to dare to own who you are.

The wounded heart says, "I have been limping for a very long time already." You may be carrying something that has never got better — in your body, in your marriage, in your mind. Brothers and sisters, this chapter does not promise you that your leg will heal. But it does tell you two things. First: that leg was touched by him, and not struck by the enemy. Second: the way Hebrews remembers Jacob is not by how capable he was, but by this — he "worshiped, leaning on the top of his staff." That staff in your hand may turn out to be the truest worship of your whole life.
9. This Week, a Few Things You Can Do

First, count how many cards are still in your hand. Write down three things you are leaning on at present — savings, contacts, ability, health. And then pray: Lord, if all of these were gone, would I still be standing?

Second, say your real name. Find a stretch of time when nobody else is there, and say one sentence to God: Lord, the truth is that I am a … — and put in the adjective you least want to admit. The blessing comes after the truth is spoken, not before.
Third, take hold of the Person, not only of the blessing. Once this week, practise a prayer in which you ask for nothing at all and say only this: Lord, I want you. See how hard that is.

Fourth, give thanks once for your limp. Find the weakness you keep asking God to remove and which is still there, and when you pray about it this week, add one line: Lord, if this is the staff you have left me, teach me to lean on it and worship you.

Fifth, tell this lesson to one friend outside the church this week, in three sentences. There is a man in the Bible who spent his whole life grabbing — grabbing at the birthright, grabbing at the blessing, grabbing at property. One night he sent everything he owned across the river until he was left entirely alone, and then Someone came and wrestled with him until daybreak. That Someone touched him only once and his leg was left lame — and yet it was on that very night that he was given a new name; and the moment he was called a winner is the moment he finally said out loud, "My name is Jacob."
Brothers and sisters, let us declare together before God:
I declare that I cannot win and that I do not need to win; I admit defeat in front of him.
I declare that I want him himself, and not only the good things in his hand.
I declare that I dare to say my own real name, because the blessing comes after the truth.
I declare that my weakness is not a mark of failure, but the staff I will lean on in worship for the rest of my life.
This week I am to "say my real name." How do I actually do that so that it does not just collapse into beating myself up?

The thing that tells them apart is direction: confession moves towards God, while self-reproach circles round and round yourself. In practice there are three steps. First, write the adjective down, and only one of them — "the truth is, I am a person who is always calculating"; "the truth is, I am a person who is terrified of being seen through." Second, say it out loud. Say it to God, and if you can, say it once to somebody you trust as well; a self-knowledge with no way out will rot inside you. Third, the moment you have said it, read a passage about grace — 1 John 1:9, for instance — so that the sentence following the truth is forgiveness and not accusation. And if you find that saying it drops you into a long stretch of low spirits, please go and talk to a pastor.
Brothers and sisters, if only four words from this lesson may remain, I want them to be the four words that open verse 24:
The flocks, sent away. The present, sent away. The wives, the servants, the eleven children — every one of them across the river.
On this side of the water there is nothing left but himself, and a whole night of darkness.
And it is exactly then that Someone comes.

Brothers and sisters, I want you to notice the timing. God waited twenty years. He had given a promise at Bethel, he had protected him in Haran, he had sent an army to meet him on the road. And he waited until this night — until the man had not one card left in his hand — before he walked over.
He did not open his mouth and begin explaining. He wrestled with him all night long.
And at daybreak he did two things: he touched him once, and then he gave him a new name.

From that day the way he walked was different. And in Genesis 33 he does something he had not once done in twenty years — he walks at the very front of his whole household, out to meet the brother he had been hiding from for twenty years.
Brothers and sisters, the man who was lamed is the man who stopped hiding.
Because once a person has finally lost in front of God, he does not have to keep winning in front of people.
Humility overcomes pride, and selflessness overcomes Satan. And this night is the picture of that sentence: he was touched and left limping — and then he stood up straight.

The focus is not on how much I have got hold of, not on whom I have beaten, and not on when this leg of mine is going to heal. The focus is on Jesus — his power is made perfect in weakness, and he himself accomplished the greatest victory of all in the place of the greatest weakness. Not I, but Christ.
May God bless every one of us this week: to admit defeat before him once, and to learn to lean on that staff and worship. In the name of the Lord Jesus Christ we pray, amen.

Leader's note: the Three Transformations are one road running downward. The first drives the point into the head; the second carries it from the head into the heart; the third carries it from the heart into the week. If time runs short, cover fewer questions rather than skipping the third — without reaching the third transformation, this lesson stops at an idea.

Priority markers: ★★★ = highest priority; if time is short, discuss at least this one in each transformation. ★★ = second priority. ★ = if time allows. The multiplication assignment marked [Must do] may not be dropped; it can be finished at home.
Transformation One | Internalise — until it becomes mindset (about 20 minutes)
Purpose: through discussion, to drive the point of this lesson home until it is a clear mindset.
1. ★★★ God waited until "Jacob was left alone" before he made his move. What does that tell us about God's timing when he deals with a person?
2. ★★ The way to win is to admit defeat, and the blessing was given only after he had said, "My name is Jacob." What does that say about the order in which confession happens?
3. ★ He finished praying and then busied himself dividing companies and sending presents. How can praying and planning live together without becoming a way of hedging your bets?
4. ★★ Selflessness is not the same as powerlessness; selflessness is strength that has changed direction. How does that definition correct the picture of selflessness you were carrying before?
Leader's reminder: the aim of this section is that people can say it, not that they answer beautifully. If someone is speaking in fragments, help him tidy it up; do not finish his sentence for him.
Transformation Two | Digest — until it becomes life (about 35 minutes · the heart of this lesson)
Purpose: through seeing, listening, thinking, speaking and doing, to digest the mindset until it becomes life.

5. ★★★ The manuscript named four kinds of heart — proud (Jacob finally got what was coming to him), fearful (I don't dare ask God to come and deal with me), ashamed (I could never say that name of mine out loud), wounded (I have been limping for a very long time already). Which are you most like? What experience made you that way?
6. ★★ Read aloud: "Your name will no longer be called Jacob, but Israel." Then tell the group: where does that sentence touch you?
7. ★★ How many cards are still in your hand? Write down the three things you lean on most at present, and then say which of them would be the hardest to let go of.
8. ★ Finish this in one sentence: "The truth is, I am a person who …"
9. ★★ This week, at what time and in what place are you going to say your real name to God? Be very concrete about it.

Leader's reminder: the questions in this section will touch long-standing weakness and an identity a person cannot bring himself to say out loud. Never say, "If you had enough faith you would be well." If someone's spirits sink after he has spoken, go to him privately after the meeting, and help him find professional support where that is needed.
Transformation Three | Transform — until it becomes daily living (about 25 minutes)
Purpose: through discussing concrete application, to transform life into daily living.
10. ★★ Is there something in your home that you have been solving by making arrangements, and have never really prayed about? Say how you are going to change that.
11. ★ The same question in another setting: at work or in your service, which card do you most often play to keep up appearances?
